When NotebookLM cannot import a YouTube link: export captions with BYTE

A failed YouTube import does not always mean you need a transcription service. Check caption availability, export a local reference with BYTE, and retain the original source link.

By At Hand Tools · 2026-11-13

On this page

  • First, decide whether you need a file
  • Export one video with BYTE
  • Inspect before uploading
  • Add the file as a source
  • Choose the smallest tool that does the job

You paste a YouTube link into NotebookLM, but the source will not import. The video still opens, and its captions may be readable. Before paying to transcribe the audio again, check whether you can save those existing captions as a file.

A reader in r/notebooklm described exactly this mismatch: direct link import failed even though they could copy the transcript from YouTube. That question dates from November 2024. It illustrates a useful troubleshooting case, not evidence that today’s service fails at a particular rate.

This guide uses BYTE to create the local file. At Hand Tools makes BYTE. The export example below is real; the notebook-upload step is based on Google’s documentation and was not tested in this walkthrough.

First, decide whether you need a file

Try the video URL directly before adding another tool. Google’s current source-import documentation, now under Gemini Notebook, supports public YouTube videos with captions. Only the transcript is imported, not the video’s visuals. Recently uploaded videos may take up to 72 hours to become available for import.

If the video is private, has no usable captions, or contains important information only on screen, a caption export does not remove those limitations. BYTE is an exporter of available captions, not an audio-transcription service.

The file route is useful when you want to inspect the text before adding it, keep a local reference, or try an alternative to a failing URL import. It is not a guarantee that every video will export or that every file will be accepted by your notebook.

Export one video with BYTE

Install BYTE: Bulk YouTube Transcript Exporter in desktop Chrome and open the video page.

  1. Find Download transcript beside the video’s channel information. The control belongs to BYTE, rather than YouTube’s own transcript panel.
  2. Use Transcript settings to choose Markdown (.md). Retain Video title, Channel name and Video URL under the included details. These English settings labels were checked against BYTE 0.9.2 source; translated interfaces may differ.
  3. Close the settings and select Download transcript.
  4. Wait for the completion state, then open the downloaded file. A click alone does not establish success.

For the live check on 13 November 2026, we opened 3Blue1Brown’s neural-network introduction in Chrome and selected Download transcript. The control changed to Transcript downloaded, and Chrome showed a completed Markdown download. No settings changes were needed for that example.

The resulting file was 2017-10-05-But-what-is-a-neural-network-Deep-learning-chapter-1.md, measuring 18,905 bytes. Here is a shortened, verbatim excerpt of its metadata header, with other header fields omitted:

# But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1

**Video ID:** aircAruvnKk
**Channel:** 3Blue1Brown
**Published:** 2017-10-05
**Source:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aircAruvnKk

The download contained transcript text after the header. We are not republishing that full transcript here. This demonstrates an actual local export, not a test of NotebookLM rejecting this particular video. The installed Chrome build still displayed the earlier extension name in its toolbar; this was not a fresh Chrome Web Store installation test.

Inspect before uploading

Open your own file and check four things:

  • Identity: the title and URL point to the video you intended.
  • Content: it contains meaningful caption text, not only a heading or an error.
  • Language: the text is in the language you expect. A translation is not the speaker’s original wording.
  • Coverage: scan the beginning and end and look for an important passage you remember. Do not infer completeness from the filename or file size.

For the neural-network example, the diagrams matter. A file of narration cannot preserve the visual arrangement of neurons or the changes in an animation. Keep the video link nearby for those checks.

YouTube also warns that automatic captions can misrepresent speech. Verify names, numbers and quotations against the video before relying on them.

Add the file as a source

Google documents Markdown and plain-text files as supported sources. Open your notebook, choose Add sources, and use the file-upload option for the .md you inspected. Check that the imported source contains the expected title and text. Use only material you have the right to upload. Google’s source guide explains the supported formats and current limits.

Keep the original file unchanged. If you add corrections or context, put them in a separate note so you can distinguish the captions from your interpretation.

A practical first question for the notebook is:

Using only this source, explain one idea it covers. Identify the passage supporting your answer, and say which details would require checking the original video.

That is a verification prompt to try, not a promise of a correct answer. Follow its citation, compare the passage with your local file, and return to the video when necessary. Uploading a file does not prove that every answer generated from it is faithful.

Choose the smallest tool that does the job

For one short passage, YouTube’s built-in transcript view and manual copying may be enough. For a local reference you can inspect and keep, BYTE supplies a downloadable file. For an immediate summary, a summarization extension may fit better.

For comparison, Glasp’s YouTube Summary with ChatGPT & Claude displayed 2,000,000 users when checked on 13 November 2026. Its listing describes summaries and transcript copying. That is a different emphasis from the file-validation workflow here; the user count is not a reliability score or evidence that either product can recover missing captions.

Start with one video. Confirm the export and imported source before trying a larger collection. If your next task is turning reference text into learning notes, use our BYTE note-taking walkthrough.
